human_tolerance.notes: Familiar to many North Americans for inhabiting settled areas near trash cans, pet food, compost piles and gardens; a slow, night-foraging animal whose attraction to roadside carrion makes it more likely than most to become roadkill.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Judgement window. 'The breeding season ... can begin as early as December and continue through October with most young born between February and June', gestation 11-13 days, young carried in the pouch for 2.5 months and left after 'about four or five months'.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Judgement window for the winter and early-spring part of the breeding season, 'can begin as early as December and continue through October'.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Judgement window for the coldest part of the winter, when 'It does not hibernate but reduces its activity during the winter' and 'It may not leave its den for several days if the temperature drops below -7 to -4 C'. The schema's dormancy name covers the den-bound period only; the animal is not in true hibernation.

vocalizations.description: Clicking sounds made with the mouth by the male, used to attract the female during the mating season; a quiet, close-range courtship sound rather than a call carried across a garden.
An open-mouth hiss when frightened, often mistaken for rabid behaviour; given with bared teeth, snapping jaws, drooling and raised fur, and followed by feigning death if it does not work.

taxonomy.note: Kerr 1792, Didelphis virginiana; family Didelphidae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 179921.

common_names.note: en/fr/es labels; the English name follows the Wikipedia article title, the fr/es labels the Wikidata sitelink titles.

range.note: Native range from 'It is now found throughout Central America and North America from Costa Rica to southern Ontario'; the pre-European northern limit is given as Maryland, southern Ohio, Indiana and Illinois, Missouri and Kansas, expanded northward since 1900. Introduced list from 'The Virginia opossum was not originally native to the West Coast ... It was intentionally introduced into the West during the Great Depression ... and now occupies much of the Pacific coast', plus the urban range extension inside the US. Koppen classes are the author's judgement of the described range.

traits.body_plan.note: Vertebrate, chordate, four-legged, furred, endothermic mammal; a marsupial, 'the northernmost marsupial in the world'.

traits.limb_count.note: Quadruped: four legs, with 'opposable, clawless thumbs on their rear limbs'.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: It walks, 'pacing' with a stride of '7 to 10 in, or 18 to 25 cm', and climbs, since it has 'long, hairless, prehensile tails, which can be used to grab branches'. The block model has no climb pose for a quadruped, so walking carries the locomotion.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a mammal that is 'a solitary nocturnal animal' and reduces its activity in cold weather.

traits.skin.note: Fur: 'Their coats are a dull grayish brown, other than on their faces, which are white', with hairless ears, nose and tail.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: 'Newborns are the size of a honeybee' and 'climb up into the female opossum's pouch and latch onto one of her 13 teats'. The neonate is developmentally very immature, but that is marsupial development rather than metamorphosis, so the schema's None is used.

traits.nest_type.note: Shelters in a den, typically a cavity in a building, hollow tree or similar: the record's Cavity value follows the article's 'It may not leave its den' and its description of the species denning in built structures.

traits.perching.note: False: a ground mammal that climbs and rests in cavities, not a bird perching on a branch.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (2.35 kg, in the Medium band between 1 and 50 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of 'Weight for males ranges from 2.1-2.8 kg and for females from 1.9-2.1 kg', pooling the two sexes.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'Weight for males ranges from 2.1-2.8 kg (4.6-6.2 lb) and for females from 1.9-2.1 kg (4.2-4.6 lb).'

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'They measure 33-55 cm (13-22 in) long from their snout to the base of the tail', the head-and-body length the article measures; the tail adds a further 25-54 cm.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: The article gives no standing height. Authored as 0.25 m, roughly a quarter of the head-and-body length, using the article's own track data ('Individual adult tracks generally measure ... 2.5 in long by 2.3 in wide ... for the hind prints') as a scale reference for the leg column; it is a stated estimate, not a sourced measurement.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'The Virginia opossum has a maximal lifespan in the wild of only about two years. Even in captivity, opossums live only about four years.' The record takes the wild figure.

traits.diet.note: 'Opossums are omnivorous and eat a wide range of plant-based food, as well as animal-based food like small invertebrates, carrion, eggs, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, small mammals, and other small animals', with 'Plant foods ... mainly eaten in late summer, autumn, and early winter' including 'raspberries, blackberries, apples, acorns, beechnuts, seeds, grains, bulbs, and vegetables'. The split of the animal foods between invertebrate, carrion, vertebrate and fish is the author's judgement, as the article lists them without ranking them.

traits.social.note: 'it is a solitary nocturnal animal', with a female raising one litter of young at a time; group_size is a judgement of a female with a pouch full of young, the only regular pairing the article describes.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'it is a solitary nocturnal animal', and 'The Virginia opossum is most active during the spring and summer.'

traits.defense.note: Freeze: 'If this does not work, the Virginia opossum is noted for feigning death in response to extreme fear. This is the genesis of the term "playing possum".' The bare-teeth threat display that precedes it is a threat display, so thanatosis is the schema's closest single value.

traits.wariness.note: Very low: it lives 'near food sources like trash cans, pet food, compost piles, gardens or housemice', and 'Research suggests that proximity to humans causes an increase in body size for opossums living in or near urban environments'.

habitat.use.note: Mostly terrestrial, moving over a 'stride' of 18-25 cm on the ground, foraging at night through 'settled areas near food sources', with the climbing share from its prehensile tail and its use of trees and buildings for shelter.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: A den, which in settled areas is typically a building, hollow tree or similar cavity; the record's shelter_tag is cavity for that reason rather than burrow.

habitat.resources.note: The fruit, invertebrate, carrion, small_vertebrate, seed and browse weights follow the diet shares. The diet's 0.05 fish share is folded into small_vertebrate, because the schema has no fish resource tag and fish taken opportunistically alongside the other animal food are the same habitat-derived resource in kind; compost is for 'Opossums in urban areas scavenge from ... compost piles', and cavity for the den.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from the lead: opossums 'frequently inhabit settled areas near food sources like trash cans, pet food, compost piles, gardens or housemice'; road_mortality High is the article's own statement that 'Their slow, nocturnal nature and their attraction to roadside carrion make opossums more likely to become roadkill than other animals in their range'; light_max and flight_distance_m are judgement values, with a very short flight distance for an animal that 'will either flee or take a stand' at close range.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'It does not hibernate but reduces its activity during the winter', so the record is ActiveYearRound with a winter dormancy phase for the period when it stays in the den.

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives a breeding season that 'can begin as early as December and continue through October with most young born between February and June', a gestation of 11-13 days, young carried for 2.5 months and left 'after about four or five months', and a cold-weather den-bound period below -7 to -4 C. The phase boundaries are the author's judgement, placed around those months; the young and dormancy phases overlap by design, since young are born through the winter.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The young remain latched for two months and in the pouch for 2+1/2 months. The young then climb onto the mother's back ... They leave their mother after about four or five months.' duration_days is the age at independence, and scale is a judgement of a young animal riding on the mother's back.

look.note: Coat from the description: 'Their coats are a dull grayish brown, other than on their faces, which are white', with 'long, hairless, prehensile tails' and 'hairless ears and a long, flat nose'. The record draws a grey-brown body, a white face and snout, and a darker, thinner bare tail, which is the diagnostic look of the species. Proportions are judgement, scaled for the long snout, round ears and tapering bare tail the description gives.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program, the only ground-mammal program available: fruit-led scavenging forage, a very short flee distance for an animal that takes a stand rather than running, and the program's default daytime rest window, which its own description documents as correct for 'nocturnal and crepuscular species'.
